topic: What if you never needed to sleep?
title: WHAT IF YOU NEVER
NEEDED TO SLEEP?

script.text: It's three forty-seven a.m. Every window in the city is dark. Except two. One of them is yours. The person in the other one is waving at you.
What if you never needed to sleep?
It starts on an ordinary Tuesday. You switch off the light, close your eyes, and... nothing. No yawn. No heavy eyelids. Not that night. Not ever.

script.beat: the fun part, with a real number
script.text: At first, it's amazing. Eight extra hours, every night. That's two thousand nine hundred and twenty hours a year. Enough class time to learn Spanish almost four times over. You master the guitar. You finish every game you own.
But here's the part nobody warns you about. Every night, the world shuts down without you. One window at a time.

And that's strange, because sleep is ancient. At least four hundred and fifty million years old. Even jellyfish do it, and they don't have a brain. The most famous attempt to skip it, in nineteen sixty-four, lasted eleven days.
So you should be the only one. Which brings us back to three forty-seven. You wave back. And across the street, the light goes out.
What would you do with your first sleepless night? Tell me in the comments.

science.claim: Enough class time to learn Spanish almost four times over
science.working: FSI Category I languages (Spanish among them) take 24-30 weeks, 600-750 class hours. 2,920 / 750 = 3.9; 2,920 / 600 = 4.9. 'Almost four times' uses the top of the range.
science.source: US State Department, Foreign Service Institute language difficulty list (Category I: 600-750 class hours)

science.claim: Sleep is at least 450 million years old
science.working: Zebrafish sleep-state brain activity resembles slow-wave and REM sleep; fish and land vertebrates split at least 450 million years ago.
science.source: Leung et al., Nature 2019; Stanford Medicine release via ScienceDaily, 10 Jul 2019

science.claim: Even jellyfish do it, with no brain
science.working: Cassiopea, with a diffuse nerve net and no central brain, meets three tests for a sleep-like state.
science.source: Nath et al., Current Biology, 21 Sep 2017

science.claim: The most famous attempt to skip it, in 1964, lasted eleven days
science.working: Randy Gardner stayed awake about 264 hours (11 days), ending 8 Jan 1964, monitored by Stanford's William Dement. 'Most famous', not 'longest ever', because other claims exist.
science.source: NPR, 'Lessons from sleeplessness: The 60th anniversary of Randy Gardner's world record', 28 Jan 2024
